With more people working from home, residential energy use has increased during what used to be off-peak hours, and commercial load profiles have changed as office buildings see reduced occupancy. Other emerging trends, such as increased cooling adoption due to more frequent and severe heat waves, are also underrepresented in the baseline model. The growing demand for air conditioning in both residential and commercial settings adds complexity to the load shapes, particularly as climate change accelerates the need for cooling solutions. At the same time, updated policies and rising adoption of electrification technologies and EVs may not be reflected in the forecasting analysis that was done in 2021. Broader trends such as increasing data center demand, industrial reshoring and decarbonization, and continued deployment of grid-scale renewables and storage resources will also impact the total system load that drives dynamic price formation. Future work should prioritize development of a new load model that includes updated meter data and the latest policy-driven forecasts for changes in electricity demands. Further, the analysis could be improved by supplementing a cluster-based statewide load forecast with simulations and other more granular datasets that allow for more fidelity in customer-level load response modeling, instead of limiting the analysis to cluster averages. At a minimum, there is a clear need for added specificity in the load shape disaggregation. This would involve differentiating between equipment types, such as resistance heaters vs. heat pumps, or full EVs vs. plug-in hybrids, as well as better capturing behavioral differences between residential and commercial users when modeling space heating and cooling loads. This finer granularity would provide more accurate insights into how different types of appliances and user behaviors contribute to overall electricity demand, enabling more targeted analysis of price response potential. 63 4.5.2 Tariff design scenarios In this study, we assessed a limited set of tariff scenarios. All scenarios modeled here assumed fully volumetric prices, symmetric import/export prices, and no additional bill components. However, real-world dynamic tariffs may have a variety of additional features, such as fixed charges, subscriptions, differentiated import/export prices, demand charges, and transactive energy options. These components introduce complexity to the tariff structures and can significantly influence the overall economic incentives for customers. The simplified assumptions in the study do not fully capture how these real-world tariff features may affect customer decisions and overall bill outcomes, particularly as some charges, like demand charges or fixed monthly fees, are not tied directly to energy consumption. Moreover, while some of these tariff features—such as fixed charges or demand-based pricing—may not directly affect load response dispatch behaviors, they will influence the overall magnitude of potential bill savings. For example, a customer might see reduced savings from dynamic tariffs if a large portion of their bill is tied to fixed charges rather than variable consumption.
